digest.title:
LP Mastermind
Market Update
digest.subtitle: What moved this week, what it means for your ranges, and what's worth talking about.

snapshot.label: Volatility
snapshot.value: Modest and steady -- most ranges likely held

digest.intro: Bitcoin and Ether both climbed modestly this week, even as AI-slowdown worries knocked chip stocks around -- a sign crypto isn't just tracking tech sentiment right now. Institutional money kept moving, but not all in the same direction: heavy ETH buying from one player, a full ETH and BTC exit from another. This issue touches Correlation, Range, Average Volume, Asset Selection, Volume, and TVL, which is worth reading closely with a Clarity Act Senate vote coming up.

stories.title: Bitmine's ETH Pile Keeps Growing -- What Sustained Buying Means for Your Range
stories.body: Bitmine added 27,180 ETH this week, about $68 million, pushing its holdings toward 6 million ETH as it chases a stated goal of owning 5% of all ETH in existence. Adviser Tom DeMark says he expects a sharp move in the coming weeks. When you see buying like this and believe price is headed higher, keep in mind there are two separate ways to lean into that view. One is picking a correlated pair -- two assets that move together, like ETH and BTC -- so both sides of your pool rise together instead of just one. The other is skewing your range higher within whatever pair you already hold, giving you more room on the ETH side so a move up captures more upside. These two levers are alternatives, not additions -- picking a correlated pair is a decision about which pool you're in, while skewing is a decision about how you set up within it. Pulling both only makes sense if you hold a more specific view, like ETH going up and outperforming BTC at the same time.
stories.spark: If you think Bitmine and other institutional buyers are right about ETH's direction, which lever are you more likely to pull this week -- a correlated pair or a skewed range? What's stopping you from doing both?

stories.title: Two Big BTC Buyers Slow Down -- Don't Let the Headline Set Your APR Expectations
stories.body: Strive crossed 25,000 BTC this week with a $36.6 million purchase, a much smaller buy than the 1,375 BTC ($109 million) it picked up the week before. Strategy, the largest corporate BTC holder, left its 845,050 BTC stack untouched for a second straight week. Headlines like these can make institutional demand feel like it's drying up, but that news happens off-chain -- it doesn't tell you what's actually trading through your BTC pools. The real check is Average Volume (45-day) -- the trailing average of daily pool volume, which shows whether this week's on-chain activity is normal or an outlier worth reacting to.
stories.spark: Next time a big institutional buying headline crosses your feed, do you check the pool's Average Volume before adjusting your range, or does the headline itself change your plan?

stories.title: Canaan Exits Its Entire ETH Position -- A Reminder That Selling Isn't Always About the Asset
stories.body: Canaan, a Bitcoin mining hardware maker, sold its entire ETH position and 54 BTC this week, using part of the proceeds to buy back 13.6 million of its own shares. That's a company-specific balance sheet decision, not a signal that ETH or BTC got riskier -- both stay comfortably inside the top 30 by market cap, the safety barrier behind Asset Selection. What it does create is a burst of swap volume: a sale this size has to route through pools and exchanges, and that extra activity often shows up as higher Volume wherever Canaan traded, even briefly. For LPs sitting in unrelated BTC or ETH pools, a large corporate sell-off like this can be a short fee-earning window rather than something to fear.
stories.spark: Have you ever noticed a fee spike in one of your pools right after a big sale or transfer hit the news? Would you widen or narrow your range if you expected a one-time volume spike like this?

stories.title: Clarity Act Heads to a Senate Vote -- Why This Might Be a Week to Widen, Not Narrow
stories.body: A bipartisan group of 17 state attorneys general, led by New York's Letitia James, is pushing the Senate to vote down the Clarity Act -- the crypto market structure bill moving through Congress. Bernstein analysts say the market hasn't priced in a surprise outcome either way, so a vote that breaks from expectations could move prices sharply. A dated event like this, where you don't know which way it breaks, is exactly when Range earns its keep -- a wider range costs some APR now but keeps you collecting fees through the swing instead of sitting out of range. Coin Market Cap's Fear and Greed gauge is worth checking too, since sentiment already stretched toward extreme fear or extreme greed tends to make a surprise hit harder.
stories.spark: Do you widen your ranges ahead of known event risk like a Senate vote, or only react after price actually moves? What would make you skew instead of just widen here?

stories.title: A Solana Treasury Company Just Set Up a $300 Million Buying Machine
stories.body: DeFi Development Corp grew its Solana treasury to 2.39 million SOL and set up a $300 million at-the-market offering for a new preferred stock, called CHAD, to fund more buying. SOL sits comfortably inside the top 10 by market cap, so it passes the Asset Selection safety barrier most LPs use as a baseline filter. Sustained buying like this tends to deepen the pools SOL trades in over time, and that's what TVL measures -- a $50 million pool barely moves on new inflows, while a $500,000 pool gets its APR flushed by the same deposit. If you're running SOL pairs, it's worth checking current pool TVL now, since today's APR may not hold once more capital shows up.
stories.spark: If SOL pool TVL keeps growing from treasury-company buying, would you rather stay in a narrower range for higher fees now, or widen early anticipating deeper, calmer pools later?

digest.closing: What are you watching going into next week -- widening for the Clarity Act vote, leaning into ETH's momentum, or something else entirely? Drop your setups and range thoughts in the group.
